rationale: A LAMBDA IS A FUNCTION SCOPE, so a name bound inside one is a local of that function and not a member of the class that encloses it. This is the second genuine ANALYZER defect the independent oracle found, and the worse of the two because it FABRICATED a member rather than missing one: in cython/tests/run/extra_walrus.py a class body holds `x1 = (lambda y_global: (y_global := y_global + 1) + y_global)(2) + y_global`, and the walrus target — a lambda PARAMETER — was published as a class member. `C.y_global` does not resolve in Python. A graph that overstates a surface is worse than one that understates it, because an overstatement sends a reader to a name that cannot be resolved while an understatement is visible as a gap. The ground truth is not a matter of convention: every row here was read out of CPython with `vars()` on the imported module — C is ['from_comprehension', 'via_lambda', 'walrus_direct', 'walrus_in_lambda'], D is ['comp', 'meth'], Holder is ['Nested', 'make']. Note what that list contains: `walrus_direct` IS a member, because a named expression written directly in a class body genuinely does create a class attribute. So the rule cannot be 'no walrus in a class body', and a fix written that way would pass the forbid row below while silently dropping three real members — which is why the positives here are as numerous as the forbids. The guard is a SCOPE test rather than a syntax test for exactly that reason, and it covers comprehensions as well as lambdas because Python binds a comprehension's named expression in the enclosing scope, which in a class body would bind into the class. The class-body comprehension case is in a separate fixture, `lambda-scope-rejects-comprehension-walrus`, because CPython refuses to compile it and a fixture whose ground truth cannot be read out of the interpreter is a fixture asserting an opinion.

_seamNote.what: A name bound inside a lambda or a comprehension belongs to that function, not to the class whose body encloses it. A named expression written directly in a class body does belong to the class.
_seamNote.why: Both constructs introduce an implicit function, and Python's name resolution inside a function does not consult the enclosing class namespace — which is the whole reason a class body is not a closure over its own attributes. The alternative reading, that the walk should treat any walrus in a class body as a member, is what the defect did, and `vars()` disagrees with it on the interpreter's own authority rather than on a convention. The guard asks whether a binding scope encloses the node instead of what the node looks like, because the two halves of the rule point in opposite syntactic directions and no syntax test distinguishes them: `(x := 1)` in a class body is a member and `(x := (lambda y: y)(1))` is not, and both are walruses in a class body.
